title: 3 — Can Quantum Mechanics under the Copenhagen Interpretation Be Experimentally Tested?
paragraphs: Maria Violaris

The Copenhagen interpretation has historically been a widely accepted interpretation of quantum mechanics. However, due to its vagueness and its inability to solve the measurement problem, a range of alternative interpretations have since been proposed and developed. These include the Everettian many-worlds interpretation, dynamical collapse theories, and Bohmian mechanics. The many-worlds interpretation, which could solve the measurement problem without adding extra structure to quantum theory, is sometimes accused of untestability, absurdity, experimental inaccessibility, vagueness, and internal inconsistency. Here, I argue that those faults are at least as (or more) prevalent in the Copenhagen interpretation as in the many-worlds interpretation. Furthermore, I use the Copenhagen interpretation as a toy model to exemplify some features of an untestable theory. The conclusion is that, contrary to the still-widespread belief among many in the scientific community, the Copenhagen interpretation has no place as an option when discussing current interpretations of quantum mechanics. Rather, it serves as an instructive historical example of a theory that cannot be experimentally tested against alternatives, suffering from the very flaws that are often (and sometimes wrongly) attributed to its many-worlds rival.
Introduction

In 2011, a poll was conducted at a “Quantum Physics and the Nature of Reality” conference.[1] Participants were asked about their favourite interpretation of quantum mechanics; a significant proportion (42%) voted for a theory that is untestable, absurd, experimentally inaccessible, vague, and internally inconsistent—the Copenhagen interpretation. Here, I argue that the Copenhagen interpretation is untestable against rival interpretations and cannot be satisfactorily confirmed. This discussion will also highlight the greater testability of the many-worlds interpretation.

Although most interpretations of quantum mechanics lack a precise, commonly accepted formulation, the Copenhagen interpretation is even vaguer than its modern contenders. This is demonstrated by the fact that it is often unclear whether a more specific interpretation—such as quantum Bayesianism or objective collapse—is a rival to the Copenhagen interpretation or merely a variant of it. The Copenhagen interpretation is sometimes identified with Bohr’s view of quantum mechanics, which remains under historical study with no consensus on his precise stance. Bacciagaluppi[2] has even argued that, structurally, it may be close to Everettian quantum mechanics: “the relative states of Everett’s theory are perfectly suitable to describe not only the empirical phenomena of quantum mechanics [...] but also the way these phenomena are seen from Bohr’s viewpoint of complementarity.” This claim stands in stark contrast to the generally held view that the Copenhagen interpretation is radically different from the many-worlds interpretation.

This vagueness presents a problem: lending support to the Copenhagen interpretation does not imply a commitment to any single, well-defined interpretation. In what follows, I explain how the lack of testability of the Copenhagen interpretation contrasts with the testability of the many-worlds interpretation. By comparing the two in terms of confirmation, incredulity, experimental tests, and selfconsistency, I argue that many-worlds is in fact more testable.
Experimental Tests

How could we distinguish the experimental outcomes predicted by the Copenhagen interpretation from those predicted by the many-worlds interpretation? Often, the distinction between these theories is portrayed as a purely philosophical matter with no experimental consequences. This presentation tends to support the notion that, since many-worlds can never be directly supported experimentally, we should accept the less counterintuitive Copenhagen interpretation. (I will revisit the problem of incredulity later.)

Here, however, I argue that experiments cannot—even in principle—test the Copenhagen interpretation against its rivals, whereas the many-worlds interpretation does lend itself to several experimental tests.

One thought experiment for distinguishing between collapse theories (like the Copenhagen interpretation) and no-collapse theories (like many-worlds) was proposed by Deutsch.[3] The central idea is to use a universal quantum computer to simulate an observer. In the experiment, this observer measures a quantum system in superposition and records that a measurement was made (without recording the outcome). Then, everything except the record is reversed back to the initial state. In a collapse theory, the quantum system will be left in a definite state (the one to which it collapsed after measurement), but in a unitary no-collapse theory the system returns to a superposition. The observer can then apply a quantum gate to force the system into a definite “0” state if it had been in superposition. A second measurement yielding a “1” would indicate collapse. Finally, one may repeat the experiment many times. A string of zeros would refute collapse theories, whereas the occasional one would refute no-collapse theories.

Using this thought experiment to claim testability for collapse versus no-collapse theories might seem inconsequential, since such experiments are currently beyond our technological reach. However, _current_ experimental intractability does not imply a _fundamental_ limitation on testability. Extreme difficulties also exist in other areas of physics—such as with respect to the detection of gravitons—that also does not render those theories untestable in principle. In fact, proposals for experiments that test nonclassical features of gravity have recently emerged that are orders of magnitude easier than detecting a graviton.[4],[5] Similarly, since the difference between collapse and no-collapse is physical rather than philosophical, it is plausible that more feasible experiments will be proposed in the future.

Other predictions of the many-worlds interpretation can also be tested. For instance, the construction of a universal quantum computer and the ability to create macroscopic superpositions are key predictions. Recent experiments have entangled bacteria with photons,[6] and one can envision a future experiment in which a bacterium is entangled with a photon such that the entangled degree of freedom determines whether the bacterium is dead or alive. If we can sustain a “Schrödinger’s bacterium” in a superposition of life and death, it indicates that life does not necessarily trigger collapse—exactly as predicted by many-worlds.

In contrast, a proponent of the Copenhagen interpretation might be forced to explain whether a living entity in superposition is possible or not, with opinions potentially divided. This very division highlights the difficulty in conclusively testing the Copenhagen interpretation.

More generally, one might ask: how far must macroscopic superpositions be taken before the Copenhagen interpretation is refuted? If we assume that the outermost environment is taken to be classical (while permitting large superpositions of some scale internally), then questions arise about why the outer environment must be classical. Since the Copenhagen interpretation does not specify when or how collapse occurs, it can always redefine its “domain of validity.” In contrast, many-worlds offers several clear experimental tests (such as simulating reversible measurements, building a universal quantum computer, and creating macroscopic superpositions) that would challenge the theory if unexpected outcomes were observed. In short, the vagueness of the Copenhagen interpretation prevents it from being tested by decisive experiments.

Even in standard quantum experiments, such as the double-slit experiment, the Copenhagen interpretation struggles to provide a satisfactory explanation. Without a detector, light passing through two slits produces an interference pattern. When a detector is used to determine which slit a photon traverses, the interference pattern disappears. According to the many-worlds interpretation, the detector becomes entangled with the photon, and one observes only the branch corresponding to the detected outcome. By contrast, the Copenhagen interpretation simply states that the photon “collapses” to one of the two possible states upon detection—raising questions about whether the collapse occurs before or after the interference would have occurred.
Self-Consistency

Beyond its vagueness regarding the domain of applicability, the Copenhagen interpretation also suffers from internal contradictions. A prime example is the “Wigner’s friend” thought experiment. In this scenario, Wigner’s friend (inside an isolated room) measures a qubit in superposition and concludes that the qubit has collapsed. When Wigner later interacts with the friend, Wigner claims that the qubit collapsed only when he engaged with the friend. The result is a contradiction: both observers report collapse occurring at different times, and the Copenhagen interpretation offers no reason to privilege one observer’s perspective over the other.

By contrast, in the many-worlds interpretation, the appearance of collapse for each observer arises naturally from decoherence—the process by which observers become entangled with the measured system, thus experiencing only one branch of the overall superposition.

Some have recently argued that many-worlds itself is inconsistent when applied to observers. The Frauchiger–Renner (FR) paradox contends that quantum theory, when used by quantum agents to reason about itself, leads to contradictory conclusions.[7] Critics have suggested that this implies an inherent internal contradiction in many-worlds, claiming that some element of observation or measurement remains unexplained. In a succinct note, Sudbery[8] explained that the paradox relies on treating one agent as a “Copenhagen” observer. In fact, while the paradox is sometimes cited as a flaw in many-worlds—even in recent textbooks[9]—its root causes may lie in a mistaken application of Copenhagen-type reasoning, as explained in Section 10.4.1 “The Frauchiger–Renner paradox” in Violaris.[10]

This example shows how the many-worlds theory has been and continues to be tested via thought experiments. To date, resolving apparent paradoxes and inconsistencies in such thought experiments has only served to validate the many-worlds theory against the inconsistent or ambiguous outcomes of Copenhagen-like reasoning.
The Problem of Incredulity

A theory’s believability—how counterintuitive or “absurd” it appears—can sometimes be taken as a proxy for its scientific validity. Is the Copenhagen interpretation any less absurd than many-worlds? Although many-worlds is often labelled as absurd and difficult to grasp,[11],[12] one must consider that the Copenhagen interpretation faces similar challenges.

One argument in favour of many-worlds as a physically reasonable theory is that multiple worlds emerge naturally in various physical theories. For example, if the universe is infinite in space or time, an enormous number of copies of our observable world (and variations thereof) are implied. Similarly, if it is possible to simulate a brain, then one could—in principle—simulate many versions of oneself, echoing some of the concerns about personal identity in many-worlds. To reject many-worlds solely on the grounds of “absurdity” would mean also rejecting a wide array of other well-motivated theories.

Another point of contention is energy conservation. While many-worlds may seem to violate energy conservation due to branching, a satisfactory explanation of how energy is conserved across branches could render the theory more intuitive.

By contrast, the Copenhagen interpretation leads to more drastically counterintuitive results. Consider Schrödinger’s cat: in the many-worlds picture, the cat becomes entangled and exists in a superposition of dead and alive states until an observation is made, at which point the observer becomes entangled with the cat. In the Copenhagen interpretation, however, the human observation causes collapse, while the cat—depending on one’s interpretation—may not. This creates an odd disparity: what is so special about humans compared to cats? Alternatively, if one adopts Bohr’s view that the wavefunction is merely a tool for making predictions (and not a description of “what really happens”), one is left with a theory that offers no account of the underlying reality. Given that many macroscopic phenomena (such as the stability of matter via the Pauli exclusion principle, or the explanations provided by relativistic quantum field theory) rely on quantum theory, denying a physical picture of the quantum realm seems even more counterintuitive than an extravagant one.

Thus, on the criterion of absurdity, the Copenhagen interpretation is arguably at least as counterintuitive as many-worlds. If we insist on demanding experimental evidence to support many-worlds—such as evidence for multiple simultaneous states of a human being—then we should apply a similar standard to the Copenhagen interpretation, which might require evidence that cats (for example) are in superpositions while humans are not.
Probability and Confirmation

The emergence of probability in quantum theory—and how experimental evidence confirms one interpretation over another—is a deep and complex issue. The status of the statistical outcomes from measuring quantum states is related to the “problem of confirmation” of the many-worlds theory, which relates to a perceived circularity in how evidence for the many-worlds theory is used to formulate the many-worlds theory.

Critics have argued that confirmation for the Everett (many-worlds) interpretation is problematic.[13] One thought experiment by Adlam considers two particular branches in a multiverse: one in which outcomes conform to the Born rule, and one in which they conform to an alternative “anomalous” rule. In such a scenario, observers in different branches would draw different conclusions about which rule is correct, suggesting that evidence for the Born rule might not straightforwardly confirm its universal validity.

However, a similar challenge exists for _any_ probabilistic theory—there is some probability that the observed frequencies might misleadingly suggest an incorrect rule. On the other hand, for a standard probabilistic theory, it is unlikely that an incorrect conclusion would be drawn (since by assumption, the misleading outcomes are the ones unlikely to be realised). In many-worlds, by contrast, it is _certain_ that there will exist branches in which the “wrong” conclusion is drawn, since even the most unlikely outcomes will be realised.

Deutsch[14] contends that our methodology for confirming theories should be seen not as a direct path to truth but as a process of testing and refining our explanations. According to this view, rather than confirming a theory through statistical evidence, we should judge theories based on the quality of their explanations. In the case of many-worlds, even if some branches appear to refute the Born rule, the overall framework remains the best explanation available. For theories based on stochastic collapse (such as many versions of the Copenhagen interpretation), the need to add an ad hoc rule to relate frequencies to theoretical probabilities underscores the testability problems inherent in these approaches.

Thus, from the perspective of confirmation, many-worlds is testable through its susceptibility to refutation by unexplained regularities in experimental outcomes, whereas the Copenhagen interpretation is less rigorously testable because it relies on an additional, less precise criterion for what constitutes a “refutation” of the theory.
Conclusions

The many-worlds interpretation is frequently criticized as untestable due to its seemingly extravagant claims. In this discussion, I have argued that the Copenhagen interpretation suffers from many of the very deficiencies it is thought to sidestep—vagueness, internal inconsistency, and a disconnection from experimental testability. In fact, when compared directly, many-worlds is far more testable than the Copenhagen interpretation. In order to meaningfully test a theory, there must be alternative theories against which to compare it. Given its vague and inconsistent nature, the Copenhagen interpretation does not stand as a viable option in modern discussions of quantum mechanics. Instead, it should be regarded as an instructive historical example—a theory that is untestable due to its inherent flaws.
